analysis.one_liner: Cuts taxes on long-held investments, limits injury lawsuits, and loosens antitrust review of corporate mergers.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 1993 with 27 Republican cosponsors, the bill was referred to six House committees and never received a single vote; it died when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill was a package of provisions aimed at making business more competitive. It would cut taxes on capital gains, dividends, and new manufacturing equipment; make it harder for the government to block corporate mergers; set uniform federal limits on lawsuits over injuries from products and professional services, overriding state law; and require agencies to study the economic effects of new regulations. Supporters argued this would free up investment and create jobs; critics could point out that the tax cuts flow mainly to investors and the lawsuit limits would reduce compensation for injured people.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors who hold assets for many years would pay sharply lower taxes — gains on assets held ten years would be entirely tax-free under the sliding scale [S2]. Corporations would get a deduction for dividends paid, an investment credit of 10 to 20 percent for manufacturing equipment, and permanent extension of the research credit [S2]. Manufacturers would get ordinary-loss treatment for failed investments and protection from liability suits [S2]. Doctors and other professionals would face new limits on malpractice claims, including shorter filing windows, caps on punitive damages, limits on attorneys' fees, and reduction of awards by other benefits received [S2]. Companies facing product liability suits would get a uniform two-year filing deadline, several (not joint) liability for noneconomic damages, offsets for workers' compensation, and a defense when the injured person was intoxicated [S2]. Anyone seeking to merge with or acquire another company would benefit from a relaxed standard that makes federal merger challenges harder to win [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Long-term investors, manufacturers, insurers, and professionals

how_it_helps.text: It creates a sliding-scale capital gains deduction ranging from 10 percent for assets held one year up to 100 percent for assets held ten years, and indexes the basis of stock and business assets for inflation [S2].

It allows a 50 percent deduction for gains on startup company stock held at least two years, and treats losses on startup and manufacturing-company stock as ordinary losses, which are fully deductible [S2].
It allows individuals to exclude up to $2,500 of dividends and interest ($5,000 on joint returns) from taxable income [S3].

It creates an investment tax credit of 10 percent plus up to 10 more percentage points for efficiency gains on new manufacturing equipment, and raises the cap on the general business credit from $25,000 to $50,000 [S3].

It amends the Clayton Act so mergers can be challenged only where there is a 'significant probability' they will increase the ability to keep prices above competitive levels, and defines market power around profitable price increases above competitive levels [S3].

It imposes uniform federal standards on professional and product liability suits, preempts inconsistent state law, requires a two-year filing window for product injury claims, makes liability for noneconomic damages several rather than joint, restricts punitive damages, and caps contingency fees for plaintiffs' lawyers [S2].
It lets taxpayers designate up to 10 percent of their tax liability for reducing the public debt, with matching federal spending cuts (sequestration) to retire debt [S2].

It requires federal agencies to analyze the health, safety, wage, and job effects of proposed regulations before issuing them, and removes the quarterly financial reporting requirement for public companies [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The tax cuts on capital gains, dividends, and equipment purchases would reduce federal revenue; capital gains exclusions primarily benefit households with appreciated assets, so the cost would be borne through larger deficits or less spending elsewhere. People injured by defective products or negligent professionals would bear the cost of the lawsuit limits directly: a shorter window to sue, reduced awards offset by workers' compensation or insurance benefits, harder-to-obtain punitive damages, and no joint liability, meaning a deeply injured plaintiff could collect only a share of damages from a partially responsible defendant. Consumers generally would bear the risk of relaxed merger scrutiny, since the revised standard focuses on whether firms can profitably keep prices above competitive levels and weighs merger efficiencies in defendants' favor. Federal health and safety rules could face delays from the new mandatory cost analysis.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and people injured by products or professionals

drawbacks.text: The liability titles would preempt state law and give defendants in product injury suits a two-year filing deadline, a complete defense when the claimant was intoxicated and more than 50 percent responsible, offsets for workers' compensation benefits, several-only liability for noneconomic damages, and tight limits on punitive damages — each of which reduces what an injured person can recover [S2].

The bill caps plaintiffs' attorneys' contingency fees at tiered percentages and makes attorneys personally liable for costs if a suit is found frivolous, which supporters called deterrence of frivolous suits and critics would call a barrier to bringing legitimate claims [S3].

Rewriting the Clayton Act standard from 'may substantially lessen competition' to requiring a 'significant probability' of increased market power, with courts directed to weigh efficiencies, would make it harder for the government to block consolidations that raise prices [S3].

The capital gains and dividend provisions would cut taxes overwhelmingly for households that own appreciated assets and stock, reducing federal revenue that must be made up by other taxpayers or borrowing; the bill contains no revenue offset [S2].
The requirement that agencies analyze indirect economic effects before proposing any regulation could slow rules protecting consumers and workers [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Some pieces have broad appeal on their own terms — a voluntary debt-reduction checkoff, a permanent research credit, and permitting labor-management quality circles under the National Labor Relations Act are not controversial giveaways. But the bill's center of gravity is a large package of tax cuts for holders of capital and a pair of liability titles that shift injury costs from companies and professionals to the people they injure, while also weakening the main federal tool for stopping anticompetitive mergers. The tax cuts are unfunded, and the tort limits apply nationwide even in states that have chosen stronger consumer protections. On balance, the concentrated benefits to investors, manufacturers, insurers, and defendants clearly outweigh the diffuse benefits claimed for workers and consumers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in March 1993 and sent to six House committees, which passed pieces of it to seven subcommittees, but none of those committees ever voted on it and it died when the Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Walker (R-PA) introduced the Fundamental Competitiveness Act of 1993 on March 24, 1993 [S1].
The same day, it was referred jointly to six House committees: Ways and Means, Judiciary, Energy and Commerce, Science Space and Technology, Education and Labor, and Government Operations [S5].

Between March 30 and July 14, 1993, portions of the bill were referred to seven subcommittees, including Tax Policy, Economic and Commercial Law, Labor-Management Relations, Telecommunications and Finance, and Commerce, Consumer Protection and Competitiveness [S5].
No committee reported the bill, no floor vote was ever scheduled, and Congress.gov records no further action after the July 14, 1993 subcommittee referral [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, existing state liability law, the current merger standard, and current tax treatment of gains and dividends all stayed in place — the main beneficiaries of its failure were everyday people whose right to sue over defective products and professional negligence remained unchanged, while long-term investors missed out on the proposed tax cuts.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Everyday people kept existing lawsuit and antitrust protections

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 27 cosponsors were Republicans, and the House's Democratic committee chairs — who controlled whether any bill reached a vote in the 103rd Congress — never acted on it.

industries.note: The sliding-scale capital gains deduction, inflation indexing, and dividend and interest exclusions would cut taxes most for households holding appreciated assets for years — gains that are heavily concentrated among the wealthiest households — while the bill provides no offset for the lost revenue, so other taxpayers or future budgets absorb the cost.

industries.industry: Product manufacturers and other tort defendants
industries.note: The product liability title gives manufacturers uniform national shields: a two-year filing deadline, several-only liability for noneconomic damages, offsets for workers' compensation, restricted punitive damages, and an intoxication defense. When companies pay less for injuries their products cause, injured people and their families absorb that cost.

industries.industry: Professional service providers (physicians, lawyers, accountants) and their insurers
industries.note: The professional liability title shortens claim windows to three years, restricts punitive damages to extreme misconduct, reduces awards by collateral benefits, and caps plaintiffs' attorneys' fees — lowering malpractice exposure and insurance costs for professionals while reducing recoveries for patients and clients.

An investment credit of up to 20 percent on new production equipment, ordinary-loss treatment for manufacturing stock, and liability limits would lower costs for manufacturers; some of that could reach workers through investment and jobs, though the tax preference and liability shield run against the public's direct interest.

Rewriting the Clayton Act to require a 'significant probability' of increased market power — and directing courts to weigh merger efficiencies — would let more consolidations proceed; if such consolidations raise prices, consumers pay for it at the register.
Capped contingency fees and personal liability for lawyers whose suits are found frivolous would shrink the economics of representing injured people against large defendants.

industries.industry: Federal laboratory partners and government software contractors
industries.note: Making cooperative research and development agreements mandatory rather than discretionary, and giving agencies copyright over jointly developed software with royalties to authors, would ease technology transfer from federal labs.
